slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?

paragraphs.text: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
Assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal and recommendation
Decision makers: the board (two founders, two investors)
Basis: Parcelbird briefing pack, November 2026 — no outside research used
Prepared for the January 2027 board meeting · Synthetic benchmark data: company, competitors and figures are fictional.

slides.title: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 — grow the software business that already sells into this market

paragraphs.text: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 — grow the software business that already sells into this market

The market is growing, but no one in it makes money. US quick-commerce sales grew ~42% a year to $5.1B in 2025, yet both incumbents lose money on every order (Zipcart −$1.90, QuickBasket −$3.40), and QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities.
Our own data say a Parcelbird dark store would lose money. At the median of the 14 sites that run our software, a store loses $6.17 per order after site costs. Our Columbus pop-up lost $12.57.

The plan’s +$2.02 per order needs every input to beat the best site on record: average order $45 vs $42, 3.5 vs 3.0 orders per rider-hour, 1,800 vs 1,400 orders a day. Miss the order-value or rider-productivity assumption alone and the store loses money.

It fails both of the board’s conditions. Even on plan, $2.5M would be left at month 18, about 6 months of runway against a 12-month floor. At benchmark economics, nine stores would lose ~$18M a year, 1.5× our cash.

Selling to grocers is the funded way into quick commerce. 9 late-stage deals are worth $0.86M of ARR, and grocers in the pipeline want fast delivery from their own stores. Scaling to win them costs ~$0.8M a year.

Decisions asked of the board:  (1) decline the nine-store launch; (2) approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires; (3) adopt the triggers on page 14 for reopening the operator question, with a review in H1 2028.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Of the founders’ three claims, only the first holds up; our own operating data contradict the other two

paragraphs.text: Of the founders’ three claims, only the first holds up; our own operating data contradict the other two
“Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year and nobody owns the Midwest”

Sales grew from $1.8B to $5.1B in 2022–25, a 41.5% compound rate. But growth has not brought profit: Zipcart’s EBITDA is −26% of revenue, QuickBasket’s −46%. The regional player is pulling back (4 of 11 cities closed).
“Our software already runs other people’s dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone”

The 14 benchmark sites already run on Parcelbird software, so our edge is already in their numbers. Their median loses $2.67 per order before any site fixed cost. Our own pop-up did worse than that median on every input.
“With density, unit economics turn positive: contribution profit per order by month 18”

The +$2.02 per order needs order value, rider productivity and density all above the best of 14 sites, a mix no site has reached. Density explains about $1.75 of the $8.19 gap between plan and benchmark.
The opportunity is real; the claim that Parcelbird can run dark stores profitably is not supported by the evidence.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing ~40% a year, but the established operators lose money on every order

paragraphs.text: Quick commerce is growing ~40% a year, but the established operators lose money on every order
QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025. The regional incumbent, the closest match to Parcelbird Now, is retreating from cities, not adding them.
Growth is not in question. What matters is whether an operator can make money on each order, and neither incumbent does.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: The plan assumes order value, rider productivity and density above the best of our 14 benchmark sites

paragraphs.text: The plan assumes order value, rider productivity and density above the best of our 14 benchmark sites
29% above top of range; 6.4× the pop-up
One-third of the benchmark; one-sixth of the pop-up
Same in every case: 27% gross margin on goods; $1.99 net delivery fee; $3.10 picking and packing; $17.75 rider cost per hour; $1.30 payment and packaging; $1.15M fixed cost per store per year.

The plan needs all four at once. The best order value ($42) and the best density (1,400 a day) were reached at different sites; no site has achieved both, let alone at the plan’s higher levels and with promotions at a third of the norm.
Each plan input is a stretch on its own. Together they describe a store that does not exist anywhere in our data.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Four assumptions carry the plan: set each to the benchmark median and the store goes from +$2.02 to −$6.17 per order

paragraphs.text: Four assumptions carry the plan: set each to the benchmark median and the store goes from +$2.02 to −$6.17 per order
Contribution per order after site fixed costs, $ (assumptions replaced in the order shown)
If only one assumption misses (others stay at plan)
Miss either the order-value or the rider assumption and the store loses money. Miss any two and it loses money whichever two they are.
Density, the founders’ main argument, explains only about a fifth of the gap. Order value and rider productivity matter more.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Even generous combinations only reach break-even; nothing in the evidence supports +$2 per order

paragraphs.text: Even generous combinations only reach break-even; nothing in the evidence supports +$2 per order
Best order value ($42), best rider productivity (3.0) and best density (1,400 a day), plus the plan’s 2% promotions.
No site has combined even the first three. At best, the store breaks even.
Take a benchmark-median store, add Zipcart’s $3.99 service fee and cut promotions to 1%, then lose 14% of orders, as Zipcart did.
Zipcart reached +$0.40 only in its densest city and still lost $310M (EBITDA) overall.
At the best composite site’s order margin (+$0.49), a store covers its $1.15M fixed cost only at ~6,400 orders a day, 4.6× the best site.
At the plan’s margin (+$3.77) it would need ~840; the pop-up averaged 280.
To make +$2.02, Parcelbird would have to run better stores than any its software has ever run, in mid-size Midwest cities.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Our own Columbus pop-up did worse than the benchmark median on every input and lost $12.57 per order

paragraphs.text: Our own Columbus pop-up did worse than the benchmark median on every input and lost $12.57 per order
Pop-up economics per order, $ (autumn 2026, six weeks, 11,800 orders)
What the test does and does not tell us
Riders alone cost more than the goods earn: $8.45 per order against $8.37 of gross margin.
Density does not rescue it. With the pop-up’s order value, promotions and rider productivity, a full store at 900 orders a day would still lose $9.71 per order.
Growth was real but bought. Orders grew 18% a week (about 180 to about 410 a day, our estimate), helped by promotions at 12% of order value and first-order credits.
The limits: one temporary site, six weeks, one city. It is an early read, but it points the same way as the 14 established sites.
The one dark store Parcelbird has operated itself did worse than the customers’ stores we benchmark, not better.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Demand is shallower than the survey suggests, and at benchmark economics a new customer never pays back

paragraphs.text: Demand is shallower than the survey suggests, and at benchmark economics a new customer never pays back
Months for a customer to pay back the $38 acquisition cost
of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery at least weekly (stated intent)
of pop-up customers, acquired at $38 each, were still ordering in month three, about 3.1 times a month (actual behaviour)

Method: $38 ÷ 22% retained = $173 to acquire each customer still ordering in month three. Each pays back at 3.1 orders a month × order margin. We leave out orders from customers who churn before month three and costs from customers who lapse later. Survey and retention measure different groups, so the two figures are indicative and not like-for-like.
Four in five customers we pay to acquire are gone by month three. Even on plan, payback is more than a year.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Even if everything goes to plan, the launch breaks the 12-month runway floor; at benchmark economics it would burn through our cash

paragraphs.text: Even if everything goes to plan, the launch breaks the 12-month runway floor; at benchmark economics it would burn through our cash
Annual result of nine stores at full volume, $M
Cash in the bank: $12.0M. At median economics, nine stores lose 1.5× that every year, before $5.4M of store capex. The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator “unlikely”.

Generous reading: treats the $9.5M as all company spending. If it covers Parcelbird Now only, today’s $0.4M monthly burn adds $7.2M over 18 months and cash runs out (−$4.7M). * Composite, as on page 5.
The plan fails the runway test even if it works. If it doesn’t, there is no cash left to fix it.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Of three options, only focusing on the software business meets both of the board’s conditions

paragraphs.text: Of three options, only focusing on the software business meets both of the board’s conditions
Path to profit within current cash
A. Founders’ plan: 9 dark stores in Columbus, Indianapolis, Kansas City
$9.5M to month 18 (plan); ~$18M a year of losses at median economics
Breached even on plan: $2.5M left at month 18 vs $4.8M floor
Only if all four key inputs beat the best of 14 sites. Upside if they do: ~+$12M a year
$0.6M capex plus ~$2.0M a year of losses at median economics
Would retest what 14 sites and the pop-up already show; scaling it brings back option A
C. Software focus, adding store-based fast delivery for grocers
Runway falls from 30 to ~26 months at today’s burn; burn must fall as ARR grows
81% gross margin; 9 late-stage deals add ~$0.70M of gross profit a year, close to the hiring cost

Runway = cash ÷ monthly burn, holding today’s burn flat. That ignores revenue growth, so it is conservative for option C. Even with no new spending, flat burn would reach the floor in about 18 months, so the core business needs to cut its burn whatever the board decides.
Option C keeps Parcelbird in the fastest-growing part of grocery without betting the company’s cash on store economics.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, and Parcelbird sells the system that runs it

paragraphs.text: Grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, and Parcelbird sells the system that runs it
ARR, $M: today and potential from the current pipeline
Why this is the better route into quick commerce
It sells into demand that already exists. Several grocers in the pipeline want to launch fast delivery from stores they already run, with no dark-store rent or capex for anyone.
It pays for itself quickly. The 9 late-stage deals ($0.86M ARR at 81% gross margin) bring ~$0.70M of gross profit a year, against ~$0.8M a year for the four hires.
It avoids competing with our customers. As an operator, Parcelbird would compete for shoppers with the grocers it wants to sign. This is our inference; the pack does not measure it.
It keeps the operator option open. Our software data on 14+ sites will show early whether store economics improve.
New contracts at $96k a year each
Conversion of the late-stage pipeline is the critical path: it funds the hires and brings down burn.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Decisions requested: decline the launch, fund the software plan, and agree what would reopen the operator question

paragraphs.text: Decisions requested: decline the launch, fund the software plan, and agree what would reopen the operator question
Reopen the operator question only if
Decline the nine-store Parcelbird Now launch for 2027.
Approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires.
Adopt the reopen triggers (right) and a review in H1 2028.
Q1: hire; work to close the 9 late-stage deals ($0.86M ARR).
Q1: scope a store-based fast-delivery offer with pipeline grocers as design partners.
Q2: plan to reduce burn so runway stays above 12 months as cash falls.
Every quarter: report contribution per order across benchmark sites to the board.
A site on our platform earns positive contribution after site costs for two quarters in a row, with promotions ≤6% of order value.
Rider pay rules in the three cities are settled and costed. Each +$1 an hour costs $0.29–0.42 per order.
Funding for an operator is committed, or the software business alone supports 24+ months of runway.
Quick commerce stays a growth market for Parcelbird, as the company that sells the software, not as an operator losing money on each order.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.

slides.title: Judgement calls made in preparing this paper (no clarification was available)

paragraphs.text: Judgement calls made in preparing this paper (no clarification was available)

Definition of contribution. The pack does not define “contribution profit per order”. We show order margin (before store fixed costs) and contribution (after them). The plan is positive on both, so the conclusion does not depend on the choice.
Reading of the $9.5M. We treat it generously, as all company cash needed to month 18. The stricter reading (Parcelbird Now only, with the existing $0.4M monthly burn on top) leaves −$4.7M.
Runway. Cash ÷ monthly burn, holding today’s burn flat. This ignores 60% ARR growth, so it understates runway for the software option.

Zipcart playbook test. We assume the $3.99 fee is all extra revenue (the pack does not say if it is net of payment cost), and hold rider productivity at the median despite 14% fewer orders. Both choices favour the plan.
Pop-up growth path. The ~180 to ~410 orders a day (week 1 to week 6) assumes steady 18% weekly growth that sums to 11,800 orders. It is our estimate, not reported data.
Waterfall order. The assumptions affect each other, so step sizes on page 7 depend on the order shown. The one-at-a-time results are shown alongside.
One-store pilot. The month-8 runway breach assumes today’s $0.4M monthly burn plus a benchmark-median store (−$2.0M a year) and $0.6M capex.
Channel conflict. The risk of competing with grocer customers is our inference; the pack does not say where pipeline grocers operate.
Source: Parcelbird briefing pack (Nov 2026); Parcelbird analysis. All figures are synthetic benchmark data.
